clinicalPearls: The commonest cause of spinal cord dysfunction in adults over 50, resulting from degenerative narrowing of the cervical canal
Presents insidiously with clumsy hands (difficulty with buttons, handwriting, and dropping objects) and an unsteady, broad-based gait
Upper motor neurone signs appear below the level of compression: hyperreflexia, clonus, extensor plantar responses, and spasticity
A positive Hoffmann sign (flicking the middle fingernail provokes thumb and index flexion) and an inverted supinator reflex point to cervical cord involvement
The Lhermitte phenomenon, an electric-shock sensation down the spine or limbs on neck flexion, may be reported
The myelopathic hand shows the finger escape sign and difficulty with rapid grip-and-release movements
Neck pain may be mild or absent, and sensory symptoms and sphincter disturbance tend to appear later

MRI demonstrates cord compression and may show intramedullary signal change; surgical decompression is the mainstay for progressive myelopathy because conservative treatment rarely reverses established deficits
reference.pathophysiology: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy results from age-related degenerative change: disc-height loss, osteophyte (spondylotic bar) formation, facet and uncovertebral hypertrophy, and infolding of a thickened ligamentum flavum progressively narrow the cervical spinal canal, and a congenitally narrow canal predisposes. Static compression is compounded by dynamic factors, as the cord is pinched during extension and stretched over ventral osteophytes during flexion. Repetitive mechanical injury together with impaired microvascular perfusion produces demyelination and grey-matter loss, particularly in the lateral and posterior columns, giving rise to the characteristic long-tract signs.
additionalDifferentials: Multiple sclerosis or other demyelinating disease
Subacute combined degeneration from vitamin B12 deficiency
Normal-pressure hydrocephalus or other central gait disorder
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the cervical spine to show compression and any cord signal change
Flexion-extension radiographs to assess alignment and instability
CT to characterise osteophytes and ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament
Nerve conduction studies and EMG to help distinguish motor neurone disease or peripheral neuropathy
Vitamin B12 and metabolic screen when subacute combined degeneration is possible
redFlags: Rapidly progressive weakness, gait deterioration, or new sphincter disturbance
Acute deterioration after minor neck trauma suggesting a central cord syndrome in a stenotic neck
Significant cord compression with myelomalacia on imaging
reference.prognosis: The natural history is typically one of stepwise deterioration; established neurological deficits often do not fully recover even after surgery, so timely decompression before severe or long-standing signs develop offers the best functional outcome.
pitfalls: Misattributing early myelopathy to ageing, arthritis, or peripheral neuropathy and delaying imaging
Ascribing bilateral hand clumsiness and hyperreflexia to carpal tunnel syndrome
Failing to recognise the risk of catastrophic central cord injury from minor falls in a stenotic neck
references: AOSpine guidelines on the management of degenerative cervical myelopathy
management: Refer promptly for surgical decompression by anterior cervical discectomy and fusion, corpectomy or posterior laminectomy or laminoplasty, the definitive treatment that halts progression
Consider a period of watchful waiting with activity modification in mild, non-progressive disease, counselling the patient carefully about the risk of deterioration
Provide supportive care including analgesia, occupational therapy for hand function and physiotherapy for gait and balance
Advise avoidance of high-risk activities and neck trauma, as minor injury can precipitate acute cord deterioration in a stenotic canal
Monitor with serial neurological examination and functional myelopathy scoring to detect stepwise decline
Manage established deficits with multidisciplinary rehabilitation, including falls prevention and bladder assessment
Escalate for urgent surgery if there is rapid neurological deterioration or acute cord compression
